claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a dual-phase microstructure containing fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves phases.
The C14 phase is Ti-rich, while the fcc phase is Fe/Co/Ni-rich.
Ti may segregate to the fcc/C14 phase boundaries.
Antiferromagnetic exchange coupling occurs between the Fe, Co, and Ni sublattices of the fcc phase and the Ti-rich sublattice of the C14 phase.
The proposed antiferromagnetic coupling is localized at fcc/C14 interfaces.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling reduces the net magnetic moment of the fcc phase.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling suppresses the saturation magnetization of the fcc matrix.
The C14 phase behaves as a rigid, high-magnetic-anisotropy barrier.
Fcc/C14 interfaces create strong domain-wall pinning sites.
Domain-wall pinning by the C14 phase increases coercivity beyond the limit of single-phase fcc alloys.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have a coercivity cap of 100 Oe.
The 100 Oe coercivity cap in single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys results from insufficient orbital moments.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys lack strong domain-wall pinning mechanisms.
The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy is predicted to approach a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
At 400 K, the dual-phase alloy is predicted to have lower saturation magnetization than single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys.
A C14 interface should produce a significant change in the fcc spin-polarized density of states at the Fermi level relative to a vacuum interface.

contradictions.description: Set B is defined ambiguously as either C14-dominant or single-phase fcc, even though these are opposite phase-fraction controls. The stated annealing purpose is to dissolve C14, which is inconsistent with making Set B C14-dominant, and the falsification rule subsequently treats Set B only as single-phase fcc.
